description: Question: why does one α emitter live a microsecond and a near neighbour billions of years, when their decay energies differ by only a few MeV? Idea: quantum tunnelling (Gamow 1928). The α particle rattles inside the nucleus and leaks through the Coulomb barrier with probability exp(−2G); G grows like Z/√Q, so a small drop in energy Q makes the barrier exponentially harder to cross. The IAEA LiveChart of Nuclides gives every known ground state (ENSDF: half-life, decay mode, Q_α); Polars and SQL compute the WKB exponent G = 2η[arccos√x − √(x(1−x))] from Z, A and Q alone (nuclear radius 1.2 A^⅓ fm). Against it, the 142 even–even α emitters, from ⁸Be (10⁻¹⁶ s) to ¹⁸⁰W (10¹⁸ years), 42 decades, fall on one straight line of slope 0.99 (the bare WKB prediction is 1; r = 0.9986, scatter 0.39 dex), and its intercept, −20.4, says the α particle knocks on the barrier about 10²⁰ to 10²¹ times a second. The empirical Geiger–Nuttall law (1911), which needs one line per element, becomes one law. Caveats: a sharp-edged nuclear radius (1.2 A^⅓ fm) and no preformation factor or centrifugal barrier (angular momentum) are assumed, so those sit in the intercept and the scatter; odd-A and odd–odd nuclei are hindered (they scatter above the line); only nuclides whose main decay (≥50%) is α are used; some half-lives of very long-lived nuclides are single measurements. Next: the decay chain of ²³⁸U, the binding energy (field binding) that makes Q_α positive above A ≈ 150, or proton emission, which tunnels the same way.
name: Alpha decay: tunnelling explains 40 decades of half-life
